title: I lost my Secret Recovery Phrase (Ledger)
plain: A Ledger is a hardware wallet: a small device that stores your private keys, the secret numbers that control your coins. You unlock it with a PIN, a short code you type in. It also relies on a Secret Recovery Phrase, a list of 24 words that backs up those keys. If you lose the paper with those words, what happens depends on one thing: can you still unlock the device? Lost the phrase and the PIN (or the device already reset)? Your coins are unreachable forever. No one can recover them, not even Ledger, the maker. It keeps no copy of your keys and will never ask you for your phrase. Still know the PIN? Then the device still holds your keys, and you can fix this. Act fast: anyone who finds your phrase could spend your coins without the device. Ledger recommends these steps: 1. Send every coin to temporary accounts: an exchange (a company that holds coins for you), a software wallet (an app holding keys on your phone or computer), or an account on another hardware wallet. Do this before updating the device's software (Ledger OS), because a very old version can block sending. 2. Delete the now-empty accounts from Ledger Wallet, Ledger's companion app (formerly called Ledger Live), so you never send coins to the old setup by mistake. Export your transaction history (the record of past payments) first if you want to keep it. 3. Reset the device. You can do this in its settings menu. It also happens automatically if the wrong PIN is typed three times. Resetting erases the keys, the device's apps, and its settings, so never reset before step 1. If you own a second Ledger, keep this one working in case you missed some coins. 4. Set up the device as new. It shows a fresh 24-word phrase; write it on the Recovery Sheet, the card Ledger provides. 5. Update Ledger OS. 6. Move your coins back, then store the new Recovery Sheet somewhere safe. Not sure you wrote a phrase down correctly? The Recovery Check app in Ledger Wallet checks its spelling and word order.
technical: Ledger's Secret Recovery Phrase (SRP) is a 24-word backup of all private keys generated by the device. If the SRP is lost and the PIN is unavailable, or the device has reset, asset access is unrecoverable; Ledger cannot retrieve the SRP or the PIN. With the PIN still known, the device remains usable and the SRP should be replaced by migration: (1) sweep all assets to temporary accounts (exchange, software wallet, or hardware-wallet-linked account) before any Ledger OS update, since an outdated OS may prevent sends; (2) remove the emptied accounts from Ledger Wallet (formerly Ledger Live), exporting transaction history first if a record is needed, to avoid later accidental sends to the compromised setup; (3) reset the device, which erases all private keys, blockchain apps, and settings, either via the settings menu (Nano X / Nano S / Nano S Plus: hold both buttons for the Control Center, then Security, then Reset all, then enter PIN to confirm) or by entering three consecutive incorrect PINs, which triggers an automatic wipe; if a second Ledger is available, avoid wiping the current device in case assets were missed; (4) set up as a new device: choose a new PIN and record the newly generated 24-word SRP on the Recovery Sheet; (5) update Ledger OS to the latest version; (6) transfer assets back, now secured by the new SRP. Ledger stores no private keys and states it will never ask users for the SRP. The Recovery Check app in Ledger Wallet verifies a written SRP for spelling and word-order errors. Restoring from an existing SRP is documented separately at https://support.ledger.com/article/4404382560913-zd.

claims.claim: If the Secret Recovery Phrase is lost and the PIN is no longer accessible, or the device has reset, it is impossible to access the assets.
claims.source: Section 'I lost my Secret Recovery Phrase but I no longer have access to my PIN or my Ledger device has reset'

claims.claim: Ledger is unable to retrieve a user's Secret Recovery Phrase or PIN.
The 24-word Secret Recovery Phrase serves as a backup to all private keys, and wallet configuration can be restored from it.
claims.source: Section 'What is a 24-word Secret Recovery Phrase and why is it so important?'

claims.claim: Anyone with access to the Secret Recovery Phrase can steal the crypto funds without having access to the Ledger device.
Ledger does not store private keys and will never ask users for their Secret Recovery Phrase.
Restoring a wallet from a Secret Recovery Phrase is documented in a separate Ledger article (https://support.ledger.com/article/4404382560913-zd).
claims.source: Link embedded in the same section

claims.claim: The Recovery Check app, developed by Ledger and available in Ledger Wallet (formerly Ledger Live), verifies that the written Secret Recovery Phrase has no spelling or word-order errors.
claims.source: Section 'Not sure that your Secret Recovery Phrase is correctly backed up?'

claims.claim: A user who lost the Secret Recovery Phrase but still remembers the PIN can unlock the device and manage crypto assets.
claims.source: Section 'Lost your Secret Recovery Phrase?', intro paragraph

claims.claim: Crypto should be sent to temporary accounts before updating the Ledger OS, because an outdated Ledger OS can prevent sending.

After transferring funds out, the emptied accounts should be removed from Ledger Wallet to avoid accidentally sending funds to compromised accounts in the future; transaction history should be exported first if a record is wanted.
Resetting the device removes all private keys, blockchain apps, and settings.

The device can be reset from its settings menu (steps given for Nano X / Nano S / Nano S Plus) or by entering an incorrect PIN three times in a row, after which the device resets as a security measure.
claims.source: Step 3, 'Reset from device settings' and 'Reset from PIN' subsections

claims.claim: If the user has a second Ledger device, it is highly recommended not to wipe the current device, in case assets were missed during transfer.
Setting up the device as a new device generates a new Secret Recovery Phrase, which is displayed during setup and should be written on the Recovery Sheet.
Updating the device to the latest Ledger OS version is recommended for optimal security and user experience.
After re-setup and update, assets can be transferred back to the device and are secured by the newly generated Secret Recovery Phrase.

warnings: Never reset your Ledger device — including by entering the wrong PIN three times — before moving every coin to a safe temporary account. Resetting erases the keys, and without your Secret Recovery Phrase the coins are lost forever.
Never share your Secret Recovery Phrase. Ledger will never ask for it; anyone who does is a scammer.
If both the Secret Recovery Phrase and the PIN are lost, no one can recover the funds — not even Ledger.
If you have a second Ledger device, do not wipe the first one until you are certain every asset was moved off the lost phrase.

notes_for_reviewer: Staleness: cached article is dated 05/13/2026 (future-dated relative to this batch) — verify the live page. Reset-via-settings steps are given only for Nano X / Nano S / Nano S Plus; newer Ledger models (e.g., Stax, Flex) are not covered — confirm whether to extend. Naming: source uses 'Ledger Wallet (formerly Ledger Live)' — confirm current branding at review time. The step-1 parenthetical about outdated Ledger OS preventing sends is terse; I interpreted it as 'move funds before updating the OS' — please verify. Source's 'compromised accounts' in step 2 means accounts tied to the lost phrase; I paraphrased to avoid confusion. Content is Ledger-specific and covers crypto assets generally, not Bitcoin only. Step 1 suggests exchanges as temporary custody, which sits oddly with our self-custody teaching; consider app-side guidance to keep that window short or prefer a second hardware wallet (our addition, not the source's). Inheritor angle: an inheritor with a device but no phrase sheet and no PIN faces the unrecoverable case — consider cross-linking to inheritance planning entries. I deliberately avoided asserting BIP-39 or any mnemonic standard, since the source does not mention them. Human operator approved 2026-10-06 (Telegram).
